one_liner: C Markdown-to-HTML library and CLI implementing original Markdown.pl syntax; converts orders of magnitude faster than Markdown.pl.
what_it_does: Discount converts Markdown (Gruber's original syntax, passing MarkdownTest_1.0) plus its own extensions (tables, fenced code, footnotes, definition lists, TOC, pandoc-style headers, SmartyPants, LaTeX passthrough) to HTML. It ships libmarkdown with a C API (mkd_in/mkd_string to load, mkd_compile, then markdown()/mkd_document()/mkd_generatehtml) and command-line tools (markdown, mkd2html, theme). Behaviour is selected per call through a flag blob (mkd_flags(), mkd_set_flag_num/mkd_set_flag_string), not a CommonMark-style options struct.
how_it_is_fast: No regular expressions: input is split once into a linked list of Line records with the leading indent precomputed, block structure is built by hand-written line classifiers (islist, ishdr, iscode, isfootnote and so on in markdown.c), and inline markup is a single-pass byte scanner (peek/pull over an in-memory buffer) with an emphasis block queue resolved afterwards. Reference links and footnotes are sorted with qsort once and found with bsearch; block-level HTML tags are a pre-sorted table searched with bsearch. This is ordinary compiled-C parsing, which is why it beats regex-substitution implementations such as Markdown.pl and Python-Markdown by large factors but not other C parsers.
when_to_use: You need Markdown.pl-compatible output (original Gruber syntax, MKD_STRICT available) from C or C++ and Markdown.pl itself is too slow.

You want Discount's specific extensions in one library: pandoc-style title/author/date headers, generated table of contents, PHP-Markdown-Extra footnotes and definition lists, SmartyPants, div quotes, image size suffixes.
Batch or server-side rendering of many documents where a scripting-language Markdown (Python-Markdown, PHP Markdown, kramdown) is the bottleneck.
Small dependency-free C build that runs on Unix-likes, macOS and Plan 9 (configure.sh plus make, no third-party libraries).
when_not_to_use: You need CommonMark or GFM conformance: Discount makes no CommonMark claim and its output differs from cmark/md4c on edge cases.

Raw speed among C parsers: in the same cmark table hoedown (0.21 s), cmark (0.29-0.36 s) and sundown (0.34 s) are 5-9x faster than Discount (1.85-1.86 s); even commonmark.js (1.93-2.09 s) and marked (1.94-1.99 s) are within about 10%.

Untrusted input in a hardened service without fuzzing of your own: the tracker shows a long run of ASan finds (heap overflows #189, #277, #280; use-after-free #281; stack overflow #239), an open uninitialized-memory report against 3.0.1 extended attributes (#298), and deep-nesting stack exhaustion (#305) only addressed by the recursion cap added in 3.0.2.0.
You need byte-identical, deterministic output: e-mail autolinks are obfuscated with random() entity encoding unless the library is configured with --debian-glitch.
Code written against the 2.x API: 3.x replaced the integer flag bitmask with an opaque mkd_flag_t blob and #defines mkd_in, markdown and friends to mkd3_* variants.

integration.form: static lib (shared with configure.sh --shared) plus CLI tools
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler and POSIX shell for configure.sh; no language standard stated (not documented)
integration.platforms: Unix-like systems, macOS, NetBSD, Plan 9/9Front per INSTALL notes; Windows not documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented; per-document state lives in the MMIOT/Document, but mkd_initialize() seeds the global random() generator through an unsynchronized static flag and e-mail mangling calls random()
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the markdown CLI reads a file and writes HTML like Markdown.pl and MKD_STRICT targets Markdown.pl behaviour, but default output enables Discount extensions (SmartyPants, tables, etc.) and it is a C library, not a Perl module

gotchas: Benchmark harness: cmark's 'make bench' runs 'sudo renice 99 $$', which sets the lowest scheduling priority (nice is clamped to 19), while benchmarks.md says the process was 'reniced to a high priority'; on a busy machine every timing, including Markdown.pl's 2921 s run, is exposed to background load. The 2921.24 s figure is also identical in every table from 0.13 to 0.29.0, so it was not re-run beside each Discount number.
The 1570x ratio is for one 11 MB concatenated document; no per-file or typical-page-size timings exist, so do not expect that factor on small inputs.
C++ callers must build with configure.sh --cxx-binding (or wrap the include themselves) to get extern "C" in mkdio.h.

String buffers grow by a fixed 100 elements per realloc (EXPAND/RESERVE in cstring.h) and output is appended a character at a time (Qchar), so throughput on very large documents depends on the allocator resizing in place (code reading, not measured).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Discount over Hoedown or MD4C only when you need original Markdown.pl semantics or Discount's particular extensions (pandoc headers, TOC, Extra-style footnotes and definition lists); for pure speed Hoedown was about 8.8x faster in the same cmark table, and MD4C is the faster choice if CommonMark/GFM conformance is wanted.
verified_claims_summary: The cmark project's benchmarks.md (tag 0.18) timed conversion of an 11 MB concatenation of Pro Git first-edition Markdown sources on an unnamed Core 2 Duo 2 GHz laptop (median of ten runs of wall time with input minus without input): Discount 1.86 s against Markdown.pl 2921.24 s, Python-Markdown 291.25 s, PHP Markdown 20.82 s and peg-markdown 5.45 s; Discount's version, compiler and flags are not stated, and the run used a 2014-15 era Discount, not today's 3.0.2.0.
status_note: Actively maintained by a single author (last commit 2026-08-29, version 3.0.2.0 adding a configurable recursion cap of 200), BSD-3-Clause-style licence and small enough to vendor, but its memory-safety history means untrusted input should be fuzzed or sandboxed.
